title: Antwone Fisher
full_review:
"Antwone Fisher" (Fox Searchlight) is the inspirational true-life story of a troubled young naval recruit's triumph over the emotional devastation wreaked by a lifetime of abuse and rejection.

Based on Fisher's autobiography, "Finding Fish," and his own screenplay, this moving account of survival and strength marks an impressive directorial debut of Academy Award-winner Denzel Washington. Although the narrative is at times predictable, the film features a commanding lead performance by newcomer Derek Luke.

The story opens at a naval base in southern California. Fisher (Luke) is a seaman with a hair-trigger temper whose volatility has drawn the ire of his commanding officer (a brief, uncredited cameo by James Brolin). Faced with the brig and the looming threat of a dishonorable discharge, Fisher is forced to attend counseling sessions with a navy psychiatrist, Jerome Davenport (Denzel Washington).

At first evasive and silent, Fisher gradually warms to Davenport's willing ear, seeing in the older officer the first father figure he has ever known. A bond of trust quickly evolves, coaxing out painful secrets from the young man's past. Through flashbacks, the cruel hand dealt to Fisher is slowly revealed.

His mother, incarcerated at the time, abandoned him at birth, just two months after his father was gunned down by an angry lover. He was raised in a Cleveland foster home, where the sadistic matriarch, Mrs. Tate (Novella Nelson), had two abiding passions: giving witness at an evangelical, storefront church and beating Antwone senseless. Soon after being released from reform school, finding himself homeless, he enlisted.

Encouraged by Davenport and his supportive girlfriend, Cheryl (Joy Bryant), Fisher begins to let go of his anger. Welcomed into Davenport's home, Fisher seems to exert a restorative influence on the psychiatrist's own strained marriage. However, when Fisher learns of the naval mandate limiting counseling to three sessions, the serenity of his fragile psyche is threatened by yet another perceived desertion. To fully exorcise Fisher's demons, Davenport recommends that he take the final step toward healing by searching out his real family.

Surprisingly, while novice Luke brings a refreshing vulnerability and tenacity to the role of Fisher, the more accomplished Washington turns in a less inspired performance as the paternal Navy psychiatrist. Despite moments of genuine emotion, a few scenes come across as heavy-handed in eliciting the desired audience response. Yet, overall, the story and Fisher's rocky journey to wholeness ring resoundingly true.

Adapting Fisher's memoir for the screen called for considerable streamlining with inevitable narrative gaps such as how the young Fisher was able to avoid the pitfalls which led his friends to crime. Viewers also may be curious about what fueled his voracious appetite for reading, writing poetry and foreign languages. Washington, an actor known for his measured subtlety, fleshes out a subplot about Davenport's previously unspecified marital problem with a closing scene that ties its resolution to his relationship with Fisher.

However, the film's cavalier attitude towards sex is unsettling. Other sailors persistently question Fisher's sexuality, scornful of how a "normal," attractive young man of 24 could still be a virgin. They are unaware of the childhood sexual abuse that fuels his anger. His girlfriend is more understanding and, although they do eventually begin a love affair (off-screen), she represents sexual healing and genuine caring rather than carnal lust to Fisher.

The film centers on a powerful message of hope, courage and nobility of spirit in the face of the most challenging of circumstances. Despite some blemishes, "Antwone Fisher" is a compelling testament to the sacred value and potential inherent in each and every person.

Due to some violence including depictions of child abuse, an implied sexual encounter, minimal rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
